title: Microscopic Anatomy of the Nephron and Bladder
subject: Renal and Urinary System (RENL)

overview.intro: This chapter covers the microscopic structure of the kidney and lower urinary tract and ties each structure to its job. It explains how the three layers of the glomerular wall filter by size and by charge, how the juxtaglomerular apparatus links tubular salt delivery to filtration and renin release, how each tubule segment is built for its workload, why only long-looped nephrons can concentrate urine strongly, and how the urothelium stays sealed while the bladder stretches. Board questions usually give a histologic or clinical finding, such as albuminuria, muddy brown casts, or a fixed urine osmolality, and ask you to name the structure that failed and explain why.
prerequisites: Epithelial types, junctional complexes, and basal lamina composition (general histology)
Order of nephron segments and the renal vascular sequence from afferent arteriole to vasa recta (UR-5)
Starling forces across capillary walls and the meaning of oncotic pressure
Primary and secondary active transport driven by the Na+/K+-ATPase
Basic renin-angiotensin-aldosterone and ADH physiology (UR-6, UR-7)

connections.how: Each glomerular disease is defined by which layer of the filtration barrier or which mesangial compartment it injures, which predicts nephrotic versus nephritic findings.
The high energy demand of the proximal straight tubule and medullary thick ascending limb explains where ischemic acute tubular necrosis strikes.
Transporters named here (NKCC2, ENaC, aquaporin 2) are the molecular basis of segment function and of urine concentration.
Juxtaglomerular cells and the macula densa are the renal sensors that start the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone cascade.
Sickling of HbS in the hypoxic, hypertonic medulla destroys vasa recta and long loops, so sickle cell disease and trait impair urine concentration.

sections.title: The glomerular filtration barrier and albuminuria

blocks.text: Pressure drives plasma across the glomerular capillary wall into Bowman space, but the wall decides what passes. Its three layers each add a different selectivity, so about 180 L of filtrate forms daily while cells and nearly all protein stay behind.

The inner layer is fenestrated endothelium with open pores about 70 to 100 nm across. The pores hold back blood cells, and the endothelial surface coat (glycocalyx) adds negative charge. The glomerular basement membrane (GBM), about 300 to 350 nm thick in adults, forms by fusion of the endothelial and podocyte basal laminae. Its meshwork of type IV collagen (alpha3, alpha4, and alpha5 chains) and laminin provides strength and a size filter, and its heparan sulfate proteoglycans give it a dense fixed negative charge. The outer layer is the podocyte, whose primary processes give off interdigitating foot processes. The filtration slits between foot processes, about 30 to 40 nm wide, are bridged by the slit diaphragm, built mainly from nephrin with podocin as a key partner. Podocalyxin coats the foot processes with more negative charge.

blocks.text: Selectivity works by size and charge together. Neutral molecules with an effective radius below about 2 nm filter almost as freely as water, while those above about 4 nm are nearly excluded. Albumin (about 66 to 69 kDa, radius about 3.5 nm) sits near this cutoff and carries a net negative charge at plasma pH, so the fixed anions of the wall repel it. Its filterability is only about 0.005 of that of water (Guyton and Hall). The small amount that does filter is taken up by proximal tubule endocytosis, so normal urine contains less than 30 mg of albumin and less than 150 mg of total protein per day.

Losing either the charge barrier or the slit diaphragm therefore lets albumin through. In minimal change disease the foot processes efface (visible only by electron microscopy) and anionic charge is lost, so albumin leaks while larger proteins such as IgG (about 150 kDa) are still retained, giving selective proteinuria. Inherited defects in nephrin (congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type) or podocin cause heavy proteinuria from birth or childhood, showing that the slit diaphragm is essential. When the wall itself is structurally damaged, as in immune complex glomerulonephritis, larger proteins leak too (nonselective proteinuria) and red cells may pass (hematuria).

blocks.caption: How a podocyte defect produces nephrotic syndrome.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading the type of proteinuria
blocks.text: A 5-year-old has heavy proteinuria with abundant urinary albumin but little IgG, and the biopsy is normal by light microscopy. Step 1: albumin is about 66 to 69 kDa and anionic; IgG is about 150 kDa. Step 2: if only albumin escapes, the size barrier and GBM framework are intact. Step 3: albumin is normally held back mainly by charge and the slit diaphragm, so one of these has failed. Step 4: normal light microscopy fits effacement seen only by electron microscopy, the lesion of minimal change disease. Leakage of IgG as well would point to structural wall damage.

sections.title: The juxtaglomerular apparatus and mesangial cells

blocks.text: The juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) forms at the vascular pole of each glomerulus, where the thick ascending limb of the same nephron returns to touch its own afferent and efferent arterioles. This contact lets each nephron compare what it filtered with the NaCl that reaches the end of its loop, and adjust both its own filtration rate and the release of renin into the circulation. The JGA has three components: juxtaglomerular cells, the macula densa, and extraglomerular mesangial cells.

blocks.text: Macula densa cells read NaCl delivery mainly through Cl- entry by the apical Na-K-2Cl cotransporter (NKCC2). When single nephron GFR rises, more NaCl reaches them, and they release ATP that is converted to adenosine. Adenosine acting on A1 receptors constricts the afferent arteriole, lowering glomerular pressure and returning GFR toward normal. This tubuloglomerular feedback protects the distal nephron from being flooded with filtrate. When NaCl delivery falls, the macula densa raises its output of prostaglandin E2 (made by COX-2) and nitric oxide, which favor afferent dilation and renin release. Renin cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, starting the cascade whose end product, angiotensin II, constricts the efferent arteriole to support GFR and raises systemic pressure.

blocks.title: Tubuloglomerular feedback
steps: Single nephron GFR rises
More NaCl reaches the macula densa

ATP is released and converted to adenosine
A1 receptors constrict the afferent arteriole
Glomerular pressure and GFR fall back toward normal
blocks.caption: A negative feedback loop within each nephron that stabilizes filtration and distal NaCl delivery.

blocks.text: Juxtaglomerular cells also respond on their own to stretch of the afferent arteriole, acting as an intrarenal baroreceptor, and to sympathetic beta1 stimulation through cAMP. The baroreceptor response explains why renal artery stenosis, which lowers afferent pressure, causes juxtaglomerular hyperplasia, high renin, and secondary hyperaldosteronism.

Intraglomerular mesangial cells sit inside the GBM in the stalk of the tuft. Where the capillary faces the mesangium, the GBM is absent, so fenestrated endothelium lies directly on mesangial matrix. Macromolecules and circulating immune complexes that pass through the fenestrae therefore enter the mesangium without crossing the GBM, and mesangial cells phagocytose them. This explains why IgA immune complexes deposit in the mesangium in IgA nephropathy, where mesangial cells respond by proliferating and making matrix. In diabetes, mesangial matrix expands and can form nodules (Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions). Mesangial cells also contract in response to angiotensin II, which reduces filtering surface area.

blocks.predict: A drug blocks NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb. What happens to renin secretion?
blocks.explain: The macula densa senses NaCl through NKCC2, so blocking it makes the macula densa read low NaCl even though luminal NaCl is high. It then signals through prostaglandin E2 and nitric oxide for more renin release.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraph on how macula densa cells read NaCl delivery.

blocks.text: Tubule cell structure follows workload. On a slide, look for a brush border, the amount of eosinophilic, mitochondria-rich cytoplasm, and whether lateral cell borders are clear.

The proximal tubule reabsorbs about two thirds of filtered Na+ and water, nearly all filtered glucose and amino acids, and most filtered bicarbonate. Its simple cuboidal to low columnar cells carry a tall brush border of microvilli that multiplies apical surface area, and their basal membrane is folded deeply around rows of elongated mitochondria, which give a striated look. The mitochondria supply ATP to the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase, whose Na+ gradient powers nearly all proximal secondary active transport. The cells also have an endocytic apparatus (megalin and cubilin receptors feeding lysosomes) that reclaims filtered albumin and small proteins. Lateral interdigitations hide the cell borders, and because it is the longest segment, its pink, fuzzy-edged profiles dominate the cortex.

blocks.text: Principal cells reabsorb Na+ through ENaC and secrete K+ through ROMK under aldosterone, and insert aquaporin 2 into their apical membrane under ADH. Intercalated cells are darker and mitochondria-rich: type A cells secrete H+ through apical H+-ATPase and H+/K+-ATPase and return bicarbonate to blood, while type B cells secrete bicarbonate through pendrin.

High transport work means high oxygen use, and the outer medulla is where supply is poorest. Medullary blood flow is a small fraction of renal flow, and oxygen diffuses from descending to ascending vasa recta, bypassing the deeper tissue. The proximal straight tubule (S3 segment) and medullary thick ascending limb sit in this zone, and proximal cells rely almost entirely on oxidative metabolism with little glycolytic reserve. In ischemic acute tubular necrosis (ATN) these two segments fail first. Falling ATP disrupts the actin cytoskeleton and cell polarity, Na+/K+-ATPase drifts to the apical membrane, and cells detach. Shed cells and uromodulin form muddy brown granular casts that block the lumen, and filtrate leaks back across denuded segments. Extra NaCl reaching the macula densa also triggers tubuloglomerular feedback, further lowering GFR. Injured tubules cannot reabsorb Na+ or concentrate urine, so fractional excretion of Na+ rises above about 2% and urine osmolality approaches about 300 mOsm/kg. Necrosis is patchy and surviving cells can regenerate, which is why ischemic ATN is often reversible.

blocks.predict: Why does ischemic ATN injure the proximal straight tubule more than the proximal convoluted tubule, even though both have brush borders?
blocks.explain: The straight portion lies in the oxygen-poor outer medulla, whereas the convoluted portion lies in the well-perfused cortex, so the same high ATP demand meets a lower oxygen supply.

blocks.text: Each human kidney holds roughly one million nephrons, with wide variation between people. Nephrons differ by where the glomerulus sits, and that position sets how deep the loop of Henle reaches and which capillaries follow the efferent arteriole.

blocks.caption: Glomerulus position predicts loop length and capillary supply, and loop length predicts concentrating power.

blocks.text: Countercurrent multiplication explains why loop length matters. At each level of the medulla, the thick ascending limb pumps NaCl into the interstitium without water, creating a horizontal difference of about 200 mOsm/kg between ascending fluid and surrounding tissue. Fluid in the water-permeable descending limb equilibrates with that tissue, and flow carries the concentrated fluid deeper, where another increment is added. A small single effect repeated along a long axis builds a large vertical gradient, from about 300 mOsm/kg at the corticomedullary junction to about 1200 mOsm/kg at the papillary tip. In the inner medulla, urea recycled from the ADH-responsive inner medullary collecting duct supplies much of the osmolality. Only loops that reach the inner medulla can build and use the deepest part of this gradient.

blocks.title: How long loops build the medullary gradient
steps: Thick ascending limb pumps NaCl out, keeping water in

Concentrated fluid flows deeper to the next level
Increments add along the loop's length
Urea recycling adds inner medullary osmolality
Collecting duct water equilibrates with the deep interstitium under ADH
blocks.caption: Longer loops repeat the single effect over more levels, so the papillary tip reaches higher osmolality.

blocks.text: The vasa recta keep the gradient from being washed away. Their hairpin shape and low flow let solute entering the descending vessel diffuse out of the ascending vessel and water do the reverse (countercurrent exchange), so they remove little more than the water and solute reabsorbed in the medulla. If medullary flow rises, solute is carried off (medullary washout) and maximum urine osmolality falls.

ADH can only make collecting duct fluid equal in osmolality to the interstitium around it, so damage to the medulla shows early as an inability to concentrate urine, with polyuria and nocturia, often before GFR falls. In sickle cell disease and sickle trait, the hypoxic, hypertonic, and acidic medulla promotes HbS polymerization in the vasa recta. Repeated occlusion destroys vasa recta and long loops, producing isosthenuria and, in severe cases, papillary necrosis. Chronic pyelonephritis, analgesic nephropathy, and obstruction injure the medulla in similar ways. Desert rodents with relatively more long loops and a thicker medulla concentrate urine far beyond the human maximum of about 1200 mOsm/kg.

blocks.title: Worked example: a concentrating defect from medullary injury
blocks.text: A young adult with sickle cell trait has nocturia. After overnight water deprivation, urine osmolality reaches only about 400 mOsm/kg while plasma ADH is high, and giving exogenous ADH (desmopressin) does not raise it further. Step 1: high ADH rules out central diabetes insipidus. Step 2: aquaporin 2 lets collecting duct water leave only until tubular fluid matches the surrounding interstitium. Step 3: maximum urine osmolality therefore equals maximum papillary interstitial osmolality. Step 4: sickling in the vasa recta has destroyed the long loops and vessels that build that gradient, so the deep interstitium cannot exceed about 400 mOsm/kg, and neither can the urine.

The urinary passages from the minor calyces through the renal pelvis, ureters, bladder, and proximal urethra are lined by urothelium (transitional epithelium), a stratified epithelium built to stretch while staying watertight. Urine may be several times more concentrated than plasma and differ widely in pH, urea, and K+, so a leaky lining would draw water into the urine and let irritating solutes into the bladder wall.

Urothelium has three cell populations. Small basal cells on the basement membrane serve as a stem cell reservoir. Above them lie several layers of intermediate cells. The surface layer is a single row of large umbrella (dome) cells, many binucleate or polyploid, each covering several cells beneath it. In the empty bladder the epithelium is about five or six cells thick and the umbrella cells bulge into the lumen; in the full bladder it thins to about two or three layers and the umbrella cells flatten.

Umbrella cells make the barrier. Their apical membrane is covered by rigid plaques of uroplakins (Ia, Ib, II, and IIIa) arranged in hexagonal arrays, forming a thick asymmetric unit membrane with very low permeability to water, urea, and protons. Flexible hinge regions between plaques let the membrane fold. Tight junctions with low-permeability claudins seal the spaces between neighboring umbrella cells, and a glycosaminoglycan coat covers the surface.

Stretch is handled without breaking that seal. As the bladder fills, the umbrella cells unfold and flatten, and cytoplasmic fusiform vesicles, whose membranes already carry uroplakin plaques, fuse with the apical surface. This adds membrane area that is protected from the start. On emptying, the extra membrane is retrieved by endocytosis. Deeper cells slide past one another, so the epithelium thins without losing contact with the basement membrane.

blocks.text: The interwoven detrusor bundles squeeze the lumen from every direction, which lets the bladder empty from any volume. Mucosal folds disappear on filling except over the trigone, whose mucosa is smooth because it is firmly bound to the underlying muscle. These layers matter in pathology. Most bladder cancers are urothelial carcinomas, and invasion of the detrusor marks muscle-invasive disease, so the thin muscularis mucosae must not be mistaken for it. Chronic irritation, such as from Schistosoma haematobium eggs or long-term catheters, can cause squamous metaplasia that predisposes to squamous cell carcinoma. The ureter has the same urothelium and lamina propria over an inner longitudinal and outer circular muscle coat, with a third, outer longitudinal layer added in its lower third; peristalsis, not gravity, moves urine along it.

blocks.predict: Mice lacking a uroplakin gene have umbrella cells without normal apical plaques. What happens to water and urea movement across their urothelium?
blocks.explain: Without uroplakin plaques the apical membrane loses its low permeability, so water and urea cross more readily and the barrier between urine and tissue weakens.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraph on how umbrella cells make the barrier.

integration.text: Histology links the disciplines of this system. Embryology sets the plan: the metanephric mesenchyme forms the nephron from glomerulus through distal tubule, and the ureteric bud forms the collecting ducts, which is why the two halves have different cell types. Biochemistry explains the barrier, through type IV collagen chains, heparan sulfate charge, and the slit diaphragm proteins nephrin and podocin, whose gene defects give inherited nephrotic and hematuric diseases. Immunology explains location: immune complexes that pass the fenestrae collect in the mesangium (IgA nephropathy), antibodies against the alpha3 chain bind the GBM itself (anti-GBM disease), and antibodies against podocyte antigens form deposits between the GBM and the podocytes (membranous nephropathy).

Physiology and pathology then follow from structure. Where a cell sits and how hard it works decide how it fails: podocyte injury gives nephrotic proteinuria, outer medullary tubules die in ischemia, medullary vascular injury abolishes concentrating ability, and chronic irritation changes urothelium to squamous epithelium. The limits are worth stating. Light microscopy can look normal when podocytes are injured, the relative roles of charge and size in albumin exclusion are still debated in research literature, and numerical values such as nephron number and loop proportions vary between sources and between people.

summary: The filtration barrier is fenestrated endothelium, a type IV collagen GBM rich in anionic heparan sulfate, and podocyte foot processes joined by nephrin slit diaphragms.
Albumin is near the size cutoff and anionic, so loss of charge or foot process effacement causes selective albuminuria, as in minimal change disease.
Juxtaglomerular cells in the afferent arteriole secrete renin; the macula densa in the distal thick ascending limb senses NaCl through NKCC2.
High macula densa NaCl constricts the afferent arteriole through adenosine (tubuloglomerular feedback); low NaCl promotes renin release through prostaglandin E2 and nitric oxide.
Intraglomerular mesangial cells support capillary loops, contract, and clear trapped immune complexes, which is why IgA deposits in the mesangium.
Proximal tubule cells have a brush border and dense basal mitochondria; thin limbs are squamous; distal segments lack a brush border; collecting ducts have principal and intercalated cells.
The proximal straight tubule and medullary thick ascending limb fail first in ischemic ATN because high ATP demand meets low outer medullary oxygen, producing muddy brown granular casts.
Juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops and vasa recta, which build and preserve the medullary gradient that sets maximum urine osmolality.
Medullary injury, as in sickle cell trait, causes early isosthenuria because urine can be concentrated only to the osmolality of the deep interstitium.
Umbrella cells with uroplakin plaques and tight junctions make the urothelium impermeable, and fusiform vesicles add sealed membrane as the bladder fills.

verify: Fenestra diameter (about 70 to 100 nm), GBM thickness (about 300 to 350 nm), and slit width (about 30 to 40 nm) are quoted with slightly different ranges in different histology texts.

The relative contribution of GBM heparan sulfate, the endothelial glycocalyx, and the podocyte to charge selectivity is debated in research literature; the chapter teaches the textbook model that NABNE is expected to test.
Albumin molecular weight is given as about 66 kDa in biochemistry texts and 69 kDa in Guyton and Hall; both are cited as a range here.
The proportion of juxtamedullary nephrons varies by source (about 15% in many review texts, 20 to 30% in Guyton and Hall); confirm the figure NABNE expects.
Urothelial thickness (about five or six layers empty, two or three full) varies slightly between histology texts.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects eponyms such as Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions and Tamm-Horsfall protein, or only the descriptive terms (nodular glomerulosclerosis, uromodulin).

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: glomerular-filtration-barrier (endothelium, GBM, podocyte foot processes, slit diaphragm), juxtaglomerular-apparatus (afferent and efferent arterioles, JG cells, macula densa, lacis cells), nephron-types (cortical and juxtamedullary nephrons with peritubular capillaries and vasa recta), and urothelium-stretch (empty and full bladder urothelium).
